name: Daria Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and a junior operator on a rubber-sheet calendaring machine. It rolls warm rubber to a measured thickness for industrial seals. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check my first sheet after a roller gap change. I like that the gauge shows whether I did the setting right; cleaning a hot roller takes patience. My husband and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. The factory pays me above the usual operator rate, we have nine months of expenses saved, and plenty of similar plants are nearby. I use AI now and then for a shopping list, but not for a machine setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew an office report may get quicker, but the sheet still has to meet the gauge. Warm rubber does not become the right thickness because a report says it did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher pay and steady orders make the household comfortable. Nine months saved and several nearby plants give us options if this one slows, even with the mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the roller gap and asking the lead to check the first sheet. I would add fresh money from each full pay packet to our emergency savings after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about regular factory work. I am not looking for a new screen when the gauge already answers the thickness question. The rubber-sheet gauge answers the thickness question without a new AI screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check after a gap change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I measure across the first sheet in three places, then look for a ripple near the edge. If the gauge is off, we stop and adjust before winding a full roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is this a new savings plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the nine months already held stay where they are. A fresh transfer would come from the next paid wage after mortgage and school costs.

say: I would **use** the gauge on the first rubber sheet after every roller change.
**AI** shopping lists have no role in my press settings.
think: **Higher** pay and nine months saved make this mild case secure.
**Nearby** plants give us several ordinary alternatives.
do: **Keep** setting rubber rollers and checking first sheet with lead.
**Save** new money from full wages after family bills.
feel: **Calm** about paid work and household money.
S0.quote: The rubber-sheet gauge answers the thickness question without a new AI screen.
fieldNote: **Daria** uses AI occasionally at home and trusts a physical gauge on the rubber line.
**Higher** pay, nine months saved and many local plants support calm and fresh saving.

steps.text: Keep setting rubber rollers and measuring first sheet with lead
Save new factory wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI may buy rubber stock and schedule jobs faster, while the roller gap still needs a safe check. I would ask for a proper paid trial before a new screen is trusted on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the physical rolling shifts to remain for now. Faster schedules could squeeze first-sheet checks, but I do not expect our higher wage or my husband’s work to fall in this slower picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the calendaring shifts and ask the lead to show me how the revised schedule handles changeover time. If the plant offers a paid guarded trial of a new AI thickness alert, I would learn its controls only after another operator shows a week of accurate gauge matches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a rushed check, though the household income looks safe. A week of measured sheets would convince me more than a launch slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a good week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The alert would match gauge readings on every first sheet through real colour and roller changes. I would keep manual measurement if it missed a thin edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would decline the new alert and keep checking sheets as I do now. Training for a company control belongs on paid time.

say: I would **ask** for safe paid trials before a new AI thickness alert is trusted.
**First-sheet** gauge checks must stay in the schedule.
think: My **physical** shifts and higher wage look safe for now.
**Rushed** checks could create bad rolls even without a pay cut.
do: **Keep** measuring first rubber sheets after roller changes.
**Learn** new AI alert if paid guarded trial proves a week of gauge matches.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed quality checks with income secure.
S1.quote: A week of measured sheets would convince me more than a launch slide.
fieldNote: Her **steady** style requires a proved week of physical gauge matches before paid new-AI practice.
She does **not** assume a trial is offered or that office automation has already removed her wage.

steps.text: Keep calendaring shifts and physical first-sheet checks
Learn new AI thickness alert if offered paid guarded proven trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my shift thinking AI reaches stock planning in 2028 when I am forty-five, and capable rubber-handling robots reach the factory around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot could load rolls and adjust the gap with fewer juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My higher-paid shifts could shrink once the robots prove reliable. Nine months saved and plenty of plants nearby buy search time, but another factory may pay less for the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and ask for a written staffing plan. If two rosters cut my hours, I would apply only to posted nearby rolling jobs with a safe role and pay that covers our mortgage and bills; I would ask my brother about his shop only if the local openings fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of paid hours, though the reserve lets us compare actual offers. I want a wage on paper before leaving this line. I would not leave the rubber-sheet press for a job without a posted wage covering our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staffing plan show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many paid rolling shifts stay, who stops a robot changeover and which workers get supervised training. A robot trial alone is not a promise of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower nearby rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my husband and I can cover the mortgage, food, travel and school costs. I would compare the actual posted wage with our budget first.

I would **ask** for written paid-shift numbers for our press.
think: My **high-paid** hours could shrink once robots handle rolls.
**Nine** months saved and many plants help, but pay may fall elsewhere.
do: **Request** written robot staffing and safety plan.
**Apply** after two cut rosters to posted nearby safe rolling job covering bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage cuts with a long search window.
S2.quote: I would not leave the rubber-sheet press for a job without a posted wage covering our mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **job** move waits for two cut rosters and a posted local role with safe duties and household-sustaining pay.
A **strong** cushion and local options reduce urgency without removing real wage risk.

steps.text: Keep paid rubber rolling shifts and request written robot staffing plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches stock planning in 2031 when I am forty-eight, then capable rubber robots arrive around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five years lets us see actual trials before choosing another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still lose junior rolling hours, but we could strengthen the reserve first. I would consider a practical machine-setting certificate only if a real nearby employer values it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid rolling shifts and add fresh money from each wage to the reserve after bills. If the factory offers a fully funded practical setter certificate on paid time with guarded roller practice, and a posted nearby setter job pays our household bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the later risk while our present wages look secure. I can make a measured training decision after seeing a real place and posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer would stop and guard the rollers before I set the gap and measure the first sheet. A video would not teach me the pull of warm rubber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course has no paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain on the rolling line and decline. We have savings, but I will not give the company free study days for its own machines.

say: I would **take** practical paid training if it leads to real local work.
think: **Junior** hours may fall later, but current income is secure.
An **offered** funded course and adequate nearby job must both exist.
do: **Save** fresh money from full rolling wages after bills.
**Enrol** in funded paid-time guarded setter certificate for posted nearby role.
**Apply** after qualification to posted nearby setter job covering bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about future robots with time to prepare.
S3.quote: A video would not teach me the pull of warm rubber.
fieldNote: She **accepts** a physical certificate after a proved opportunity, fitting steady adaptability.
**Funding**, paid guarded practice and a posted adequate local job condition both training and application.

steps.text: Save new rolling wages after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches stock planning in 2036 when I am fifty-three, with capable rubber robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. A decade gives paid years to save and learn before the physical line changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older, but we will still need wages after fifty-six. Our nine-month reserve is a buffer, not retirement money, and a nearby factory only helps if its posted wage covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep rolling shifts and add new pay to savings after bills. I would ask the lead for practical gap-setting lessons now; if the factory later offers fully funded paid-time guarded setter training and a posted nearby job at adequate pay, I would qualify and apply after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about eventual hours cuts, though the household is secure today. A long warning is useful only if I keep checking real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change house plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paying the current mortgage rather than assume we can move when the children are older. We would revisit it only after a real wage change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn an AI control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a paid demonstration and require a week of measured results first. I would learn a new alert only if an offered guarded paid place follows those checks.

think: Our household will still depend on **factory wages** after age fifty-six.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant cuts with current finances secure.
S4.quote: Our nine-month reserve is a buffer, not retirement money, and a nearby factory only helps if its posted wage covers our mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because rubber-handling robots around 2031 could cut my higher-paid shifts. Written staffing terms and posted nearby safe jobs paying our mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person checking a rubber sheet gets a paid hour to learn the next machine. I learned from people who worked beside me, and the new operator should get that chance. A gauge is honest about a thin sheet even when an office report is confident.

headlineQuote: A gauge is honest about a thin sheet even when an office report is confident.
portrait: **Daria**, forty-three, is a junior rubber-sheet operator with secondary schooling and two school-age children.
Her **higher** wage, nine-month reserve and many nearby plants give the household substantial choices.
She **uses** AI occasionally outside work and waits for measured proof before learning a new control.
She **values** paid practical learning and applies only to posted safe local work that covers household bills.
biggestWorry: **Fast** rubber-handling robots around 2031 could reduce Daria’s higher-paid junior shifts.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** staffing terms and a posted nearby safe job paying mortgage and bills would help.
